section.title: Derivatives and Integrals of Vector Functions

content.paragraph: Later in this chapter we are going to use vector functions to describe the motion of planets and other objects through space. Here we prepare the way by developing the calculus of vector functions.

If the points $$P$$ and $$Q$$ have position vectors $$\mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.$$ and $$\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right.$$ , then $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ represents the vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right. - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.$$ , which can therefore be regarded as a secant vector. If $$h > 0$$ , the scalar multiple $$\left( {1 \slash h}) \right.\left( {\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right. - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.}) \right.$$ has the same direction as $$\mathbf{r}\left( {t + h}) \right. - \mathbf{r}\left( t) \right.$$ . As $$\left. h\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , it appears that this vector approaches a vector that lies on the tangent line. For this reason, the vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.$$ is called the tangent vector to the curve defined by $$\mathbf{r}$$ at the point $$P$$ , provided that $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.$$ exists and $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right. \neq 0$$ . The tangent line to $$C$$ at $$P$$ is defined to be the line through $$P$$ parallel to the tangent vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\left( t) \right.$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Geometrically, Theorem 4 says that if a curve lies on a sphere with center the origin, then the tangent vector $$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}$$ is always perpendicular to the position vector $$\mathbf{r}{(t)}$$ . (See Figure 4.)
